body_markdown:
The more middle-aged among us may recall the once-popular local advertiser’s matchbook tagline: “You’ve tried the rest, so now, why not the best?” Looking at my fleet and thinking of the many fine machines I’ve had to let go over the years when funds ran low, I realize I’ve turned that chestnut on its head more than once. Now I say to myself: “You’ve tried the best, so now, why not the rest?”


Which brings me to my very own 1969 Triumph 1300, a car I imported from England about five years ago and now, with great sadness, reluctantly plan to part with. Never sold in the U.S., it’s a car so obscure that many dedicated American fans of British cars haven’t even heard of it. Which to me doesn’t undersell it. Because it’s a delightful, rolling window into a troubled but commendably ambitious carmaker’s fascinating history. And as a serial Triumph owner and all-around car bore, it’s a tale I feel compelled to share.


Jamie Kitman


The story begins in 1903 with the Standard Motor Co. The word “standard” had no downscale connotation in the King’s English then, though that changed over time, as in America, where “standard” became synonymous with “ordinary.” Its fortunes flagging, in 1945, Standard acquired another English car and motorcycle maker, Triumph, whose two Coventry plants had been bombed within an inch of their lives in WWII. In time, the blended company started calling all of its cars Triumphs, while unrelated owners continued to make Triumph motorcycles.


By the 1960s, Triumph cars had proven successful where staid Standards hadn’t—at home and especially in the U.S. export market—where its TR line of sports cars were well-regarded for speed, value, and sporty good looks. Credit for the company’s comeback and stylistic renaissance increasingly belonged to the Italian stylist Giovanni Michelotti, who would in his day pen not just a host of extraordinarily attractive Triumph sports cars, (Spitfire, TR4/5/250, Stag, and the TR3-based Italia)[but also](https://www.classicandsportscar.com/gallery/24-memorable-michelotti-classics) the BMW 1500/2000 and 2002, Alpine A110, Maserati 3500GT convertible, Ferrari 212 Inter, and DAF 44.


A new Triumph Herald leaves the showrooms of King and Harper on Milton Road Cambridge, May 1959.


Getty Images


Of moment here, the chain-smoking Michelotti also designed for Triumph a plucky entry-level model, the Herald. Debuting for 1960, it provided healthy sales for a time, along with the related and even more adorable Spitfire two-seater based upon it. With the firm’s brawnier TR roadsters, these were the Triumphs which most captivated Americans in the 1960s. Though it would sell well at home, problems with the Herald (later renamed 13/60) were hardly unknown, one important issue stemming from its spindly body-on-frame design. Limited factory resources saw three body sections supplied from different pressing plants, delivered to the Triumph plant in Canley, where they were bolted together to cloak the frame. This arguably made repairs more convenient, an unexpected long-term benefit for dedicated owners, for as it turned out the sheet metal rusted readily. However, the model’s Erector Set construction also ensured an inevitable rising tide of rattles, creaks, and ill-fitting doors as the cars aged and sagged. Clever and much-loved nonetheless, the Herald embodied what would become a persistent Triumph hallmark: making the most out of the least.


Underwritten by British truck maker Leyland, which purchased Triumph in 1960, here was a firm endeavoring to make cars that on paper would stand with or above its larger and richer homegrown competition. Technically adventurous, then-giant BMC took occasional swings at avant garde things like unit bodies, front-wheel drive, fluid suspension, and transverse engines, while well-heeled Ford of England had the unit bodies down pat but stuck successfully with conventional drivetrains, solid rear axles, and longitudinal powerplants for models in every shape, size, and color. Along with General Motors’ conservative Vauxhall, they put Triumph in a precarious box, leading the smaller Coventry firm’s owners to conclude they must move upscale to achieve profitability. And to justify higher prices in a deeply cost-conscious postwar Britain, Triumph rolled out every modern technology its ambitious engineers could concoct—at least the ones they could afford. Experiments with Italian design, targa roofs, independent rear suspension, and fuel injection all evidenced the small company’s desire to punch above its weight.


Shared with the Spitfire, the Herald’s IRS, for instance, was now a marketable attribute and a step forward in ride comfort. But a cost-saving swing-axle design meant rear wheels and tires were prone to winding up in vigorous cornering as they tucked under, leading to outrageous positive camber angles and violent snap understeer that caused cars so challenged to keep stepping—hopping, really—right off the road. Later Heralds and Spitfires sought to address the problem, though these arrangements remained less than ideal.


A more technologically successful early fruit of the new energy around Triumph came with the launch of the Michelotti-designed 2000 for the 1964 model year. A smart-looking four-door of unibody construction, its 2.0-liter six-cylinder power, improved IRS, and luxurious, wood-lined interior made it a serious contender in the emerging executive class. Reception by the press and public was encouraging, and a few even made it to the U.S. Hopes ran high.


Triumph 1300 on display at the London Motor Show at Earls Court on October 20, 1965.


Sutton Images


Around the same time, it was clear the Herald would need replacing. In keeping with Triumph’s new tradition of engineering innovation on a shoestring, in 1962 the firm had launched Project Ajax. With Michelotti once again masterminding the design, which recalled the 2000, the new, smaller, four-door 1300, which launched in 1965, was treated not only to a rigid unit body but arranged to repurpose the 1296-cc four found in the Spitfire and Herald to power its front wheels—a first for Triumph and potential cost-saver, too.


Rotated 180 degrees so that its flywheel was at the front of the car, it was another clever example of bold, situational thinking. While liberal use of the Triumph parts bin was in order, money was also found for niceties like double wishbones up front and semi-trailing arm independent rear suspension, which made for a much better handling machine than the Herald, augmented by excellent direct steering, and that rigid body shell.


Triumph 1300 bodies on the production line at the Standard Triumph assembly facility in Speke, Liverpool, February 1968.


Getty Images


Inside the 1300, the march upscale was made even clearer, as solid wood—not veneer—abounded, making for dash and door trim above the car’s station in life. A comfortable, spacious cabin, with generously sized front bucket seats in premium leather-look vinyl, a big trunk (er, boot), and a full array of round gauges brought the English drawing room vibe to a motorway-capable fuel sipper that looked modern, yet adorably cute. Michelotti had struck again. Because of its many additional accoutrements, it was more costly than the Herald, which soldiered on until 1970 as a low-price alternative alongside the 1300, now archaically named 13/60. Triumph managed to sell close to 150,000 copies of the 1300 in three years, respectable for what was essentially a new type of car—the premium economy car.


Leather-look vinyl and real wood inserts gave the 1300 a real touch of class.


Jamie Kitman


And now for something completely different…


Underscoring how far outside of the packing crate Triumph was marching, the original 1300 was followed by a redesigned model, the Toledo, that could, until 1973, be bought as the 1300’s mildly facelifted successor. There was a longer-bodied variant as well, the 1500, in either front- or rear-wheel-drive form. Also sharing a longer-body version of the platform—craftily updated by Michelotti—would come the 1972–80 Dolomite. A sporty[Dolomite Sprint](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/buying-guide-triumph-dolomite-sprint/) version, which made headlines beginning in 1972, also ran through 1980. Rear-wheel-drive only and blessed with 130-or-so horsepower from a 16-valve SOHC 2-liter engine, it was a serious express machine.


Triumph


Triumph


I know this for a fact, as I owned a Dolomite Sprint for years, brought from an ex-Triumph factory worker in England who’d had the foresight to stash a fresh body shell away when production ended, and it’s still out there in good hands with my Michigan-based friend, Rusty Blackwell. Writing in the pages of *[Automobile](https://web.archive.org/web/20100817054829/http:/www.automobilemag.com/reviews/driven/1004_triumph_dolomite_sprint_vs_bmw_2002tii/the_ultimate_driving_machine.html)*[magazine](https://web.archive.org/web/20100817054829/http:/www.automobilemag.com/reviews/driven/1004_triumph_dolomite_sprint_vs_bmw_2002tii/the_ultimate_driving_machine.html) in 2010, I made the argument that Triumph, properly managed and funded, could have been Britain’s answer to BMW. But by 1968, Triumph had been swallowed whole by British Leyland, the unmanageable conglomerate under whose flag so many legendary English brands combined before dying swift or, as in Triumph’s case, slow, painful deaths. Over the course of the article, I confessed to liking the Dolomite better than the lovely 2002tii I owned simultaneously. That very Dolomite Sprint, by crazy coincidence, was made into a 1/43-scale Corgi model earlier this century, when Corgi designers saw it at a car show in England shortly before I bought it.


Jamie Kitman


Triumph never followed up on the 1300 or its derivatives, its last sedan being a lightly rebadged Honda Civic called the Acclaim, which ran from 1981 to 1984. But speaking of miniature cars, I first fell in love with the 1300, which I’d never heard of despite a childhood fascination with British cars, when I came across (and persuaded my mother to pay for) a Dinky car version when my parents took me and my sisters to London in 1971 for our first travel abroad. I still have the model today, which I found in a glass display case at the Hamleys toy store on Regent Steet. For now, it will have to do, as my full-size 1300 is going up for sale on Hagerty Marketplace very soon.


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


A rust-free old lady’s car with 43,000 original miles and an excellent interior, it has benefited during my ownership from a new clutch, rebuilt steering rack, brake work, exhaust, and a carburetor rebuild. It’s a delight to drive, blessed of a luxurious yet mildly sporting character. It’s no tire shredder but it’s a torquey, very British thing that keeps up with traffic and rolls down the interstate at 65–70 mph without complaint. It’s a Triumph 1300 as close to original as you will find, it’s here in America, and as you hold your head regally high, chin up, you will agree there’s nothing standard about it.


Jamie Kitman


***


*A man of many pursuits (rock band manager, automotive journalist, concours judge, purveyor of picture cars for film and TV), Jamie Kitman lives and breathes vintage machines.
